title: Close House Race in Southwest Washington Could Help Decide Congress
summary:
One of the tightest U.S. House races this year is in Washington state's 3rd Congressional District, a mix of cities, factories, farms, and coastal towns. Control of the House of Representatives could partly depend on who wins there.

Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez flipped the seat blue in 2022, even though President Trump has won the district three times. Her Republican challenger is state Sen. John Braun, who owns a small company that builds emergency vehicles. Both candidates describe themselves as moderates who back manufacturing, natural resources, and small businesses.

Braun told NPR the district is not predictable and candidates must earn votes. Longview Mayor Erik Halvorson said voters often split tickets: Trump can win the area while Gluesenkamp Perez also wins on the same ballot. He said people want leaders who show up and understand local problems.

Local issues include tariffs that raise costs for builders and exporters, housing prices in growing Vancouver, and tough times for coastal shellfish farms and fishing towns. Kathleen Nisbet, who runs Goose Point Oysters in Bay Center, said her farm faces many agency fees and has lost more than half of its international sales amid trade tensions with Asian countries. Ilwaco, once centered on natural resources, now leans more on tourism and hospitality.

Some Democrats in Clark County are unhappy with Gluesenkamp Perez over certain votes, and she faced a left-leaning primary challenge before advancing. She defended a vote for the SAVE Act, saying she supports requiring that only U.S. citizens vote. Braun has Trump's endorsement but says he would break with broad, "indiscriminate" tariffs.

Both sides see the seat as important: Democrats want to keep it to chase a House majority, while Republicans want it to help advance Trump's agenda.
why_it_matters: Close House races decide who writes national laws on jobs, trade, and services. Kids can see how local factories, farms, and towns connect to Congress.

background_read: The U.S. House of Representatives is divided into districts, and each district elects one member.
A competitive district can still vote for different parties for president and for Congress on the same ballot.
Local economies—factories, farms, ports, and small towns—often shape what voters care about most.
Control of the House depends on winning many such seats across the country.
